items.question: In one sentence: who does a carrier-side dispatcher work for, and what is their main goal?
items.answer: For a motor carrier . Main goal: keep the carrier’s trucks loaded with profitable, legal freight, and get the loads delivered and paid.

items.question: Name three things the carrier supplies that you should not buy at the start.
items.answer: Any three of: truck/trailer, operating authority (USDOT/MC), insurance, a load-board subscription or seat, the ELD/tracking system.

items.question: A friend offers you his DAT username and password “so you can practice.” What do you say, and why?
items.answer: “No, thanks.” Shared logins break platform rules, can be seen as fraud, and every search would be under someone else’s identity. Access should come from a carrier or employer, as your own seat.

items.question: It is October. An Atlanta, GA broker says “call me back at 2 PM.” What time is that in Pakistan?
items.answer: October = daylight saving time. Atlanta is Eastern: PKT = ET + 9. 2 PM ET = 11 PM PKT .

items.question: It is January. A Los Angeles receiver opens at 7 AM. What time is that in Pakistan?
items.answer: January = standard time. Los Angeles is Pacific: PKT = PT + 13. 7 AM PT = 8 PM PKT , same day.

items.question: Why do small carriers (the 91.5%) need dispatchers?
items.answer: Owners with 10 or fewer trucks often drive themselves or have no office staff. They can’t search, call and do paperwork while driving, and empty days cost them money.

items.question: True or false: “There is a federal dispatcher license you must get first.” Explain.
items.answer: False. There is no federal dispatcher license. But if your activities are brokerage, you need broker registration.

items.question: The best-paying load on the board goes to a city where trucks rarely find a next load. Is it automatically the best choice? Why?
items.answer: No. A dead market can mean a long empty drive or a cheap load to get out again. Always consider the next load and the empty miles (Module 7).

items.question: What is the most common barrier in Pakistani dispatch job ads, and what is your plan to get past it?
items.answer: 6–12 months’ experience. Plan: build portfolio evidence (mock calls, RC review, simulation log), target entry roles, and apply after Module 8.

items.question: Write a pickup time correctly for your notes: pickup is Thursday 9 AM Central, in summer.
items.answer: “PU Thu 9:00 AM CT (Thu 7:00 PM PKT)” — summer: PKT = CT + 10.

items.question: Put these in order: carrier, receiver, broker, shipper. Where does the dispatcher sit?
items.answer: Shipper → broker → carrier → receiver. The dispatcher sits inside the carrier .

items.question: Who creates the BOL, and who creates the RC?
items.answer: The shipper creates the BOL. The broker creates the RC.

items.question: What turns a BOL into a POD?
items.answer: The receiver’s signature (usually with date, count and stamp) at delivery.

items.question: Load #12354 paid $700 for 240 miles. What is the rate per loaded mile? And the rate per total mile if the truck drove 80 empty miles first?
items.answer: $700 ÷ 240 = $2.92 per loaded mile. $700 ÷ 320 = $2.19 per total mile.

items.question: Name the three penalties or risks written in the Ship Express RC.
items.answer: MacroPoint tracking required ($150 deduction), POD within 72 h ($150 deduction), no TONU pay if the load is cancelled.

items.question: Why does the money flow “in the opposite direction and later”? What problem does factoring solve?
items.answer: The broker pays after the job is done and the paperwork arrives, often weeks later. Factoring gives the carrier cash in a day or two, for a fee.

items.question: Delivery is 12 PM Central in Owensboro. What time is that in Eastern Time? And in Pakistan in February?
items.answer: 12 PM CT = 1 PM ET . In February (standard time) PKT = CT + 11, so 11 PM PKT .

items.question: Give two reasons to get a photo of the BOL before the driver leaves the shipper.
items.answer: To compare it with the RC (count, weight, address) while problems can still be fixed at the shipper, and to have proof of what was loaded in case of a later dispute.

items.question: What must you do immediately if a receiver writes “1 pallet damaged” on the POD?
items.answer: Call the broker immediately, inform the carrier, and get photos of the freight and the signed POD. Document everything for a possible claim.

items.question: Name four activities that turn a “dispatcher” into an unregistered broker.
items.answer: Any four: negotiating directly with shippers; taking pay from a broker or factor; accepting a load before having a truck; allocating a load between carriers; handling broker-to-carrier payments.

items.question: Who should pay a carrier-side dispatcher?
items.answer: The carrier only , or your employer, which is paid by its carriers.

items.question: Explain the difference between a driver’s check call and a broker update.
items.answer: A check call is you getting status from the driver (location, loaded, count, ETA). A broker update is you telling the broker that status, proactively.

items.question: What is the difference between a tractor-trailer and a straight truck, and why does it matter for drop-and-hook loads?
items.answer: A tractor-trailer is two units: the tractor can drop one trailer and hook another. A straight truck’s box is on the same frame and can’t be dropped. Drop-and-hook and power-only work need a tractor.

items.question: The federal gross limit is 80,000 lb. Why can’t a 53′ dry van usually carry 80,000 − 0 lb of cargo? Give the example math.
items.answer: 80,000 lb is the gross for the whole vehicle. Example: 80,000 − tractor/fuel/driver 19,000 − trailer 15,000 = 46,000 lb on paper, and axle limits and real loading usually make it less. Ask the carrier for the truck’s max.

items.question: How many 48″ × 40″ pallets fit in a 53′ van straight? Turned? In a 26′ box truck?
items.answer: 26 straight, up to 30 turned (if the inside width and loading allow); about 12 in a 26′ box truck.

items.question: True or false: “The federal height limit is 13′6″.” Explain.
items.answer: False. There is no federal vehicle height limit. States set limits, mostly 13′6″–14′, and routes can be lower.

items.question: A 26′ box truck has a GVWR of 25,999 lb. Does the driver need a CDL to haul general freight? What if the GVWR were 33,000 lb?
items.answer: 25,999 lb GVWR, no hazmat → usually no CDL . 33,000 lb GVWR → Class B CDL . Length doesn’t decide it.

items.question: Name four things you ask before booking a box truck to a residential address.
items.answer: Any four: dock or no dock; residential?; liftgate required?; pallet jack?; forklift on site?; heaviest pallet weight vs liftgate capacity; inside dimensions.

items.question: Explain continuous vs cycle mode, and who decides which is used.
items.answer: Continuous: the unit runs all the time. Cycle/start-stop: it switches off at the setpoint and restarts as needed. The shipper decides; it’s usually on the RC or BOL.

items.question: What does FDA’s rule say about pre-cooling? What was wrong with the old manual rule?
items.answer: The compartment must be adequately prepared, “including precooling, if necessary.” The old “always 2 hours” rule is not in the regulation. Follow the shipper’s instructions.

items.question: A 25-ft article on a flatbed, not blocked: minimum number of tiedowns under FMCSA’s general rule?
items.answer: First 10 ft → 2; remaining 15 ft → 2 more (10 + 5) = 4 tiedowns minimum, plus any commodity-specific rules.

items.question: A machine is 9′10″ tall. Flatbed deck 5′0″, step-deck lower deck 3′4″. What is the loaded height on each, and which could be legal where the limit is 13′6″?
items.answer: Flatbed: 5′0″ + 9′10″ = 14′10″ ✗. Step deck: 3′4″ + 9′10″ = 13′2″ ✓ under 13′6″, if every state and bridge on the route allows it.

items.question: What do MV, VH, VM and VC mean on DAT today?
items.answer: MV = Moving Van · VH = Van Hotshot · VM = Van w/ Team · VC = Van w/ Curtains.

items.question: What must be true before you book a placarded hazmat load?
items.answer: The driver has a hazmat endorsement and the carrier is set up for hazmat (registration, insurance, procedures), and the truck can be placarded correctly. Otherwise, don’t book.

items.question: What do odd and even interstate numbers tell you? Where would you expect I-5 and I-95?
items.answer: Odd = north–south, even = east–west. I-5 on the West Coast (lowest odd, far west); I-95 on the East Coast.

items.question: What does a three-digit interstate starting with an even digit usually mean? With an odd digit?
items.answer: Even first digit: loop or connector around/through a city (I-285). Odd first digit: spur off the main route (I-575).

items.question: Name the main interstate(s) for Dallas → Atlanta, and the time zone of each city.
items.answer: I-20 almost all the way. Dallas = Central, Atlanta = Eastern.

items.question: Which DAT zone would you search for loads going to Texas or Oklahoma?
items.answer: Z7 (AR, LA, OK, TX).

items.question: Why is Laredo important to U.S. trucking, and which interstate starts there?
items.answer: It is the busiest U.S.–Mexico land port for freight; cross-border freight flows north on I-35.

items.question: Give two differences between a truck route and a car route.
items.answer: Any two: truck GPS avoids low bridges and weight limits; trucks are banned from some roads (e.g. NY parkways); hazmat routes; road miles for rates come from truck mileage systems.

items.question: What is the difference between a freight hub and a “hot market”?
items.answer: A hub produces freight all year (e.g. Chicago, Atlanta). A hot market has more loads than trucks right now, and changes week to week.

items.question: Delivery is Monday 4:00 PM Eastern in January. What is that in Pakistan time, including the day?
items.answer: January = winter, ET +10: 4 PM ET → 2 AM Tuesday PKT .

items.question: Why does Phoenix have the same clock as Los Angeles in summer but not in winter?
items.answer: Arizona (mostly) doesn’t use DST: it stays on MST (UTC−7). In summer California is on PDT (also UTC−7); in winter California is on PST (UTC−8).

items.question: Name three states that have two time zones, and one city in each zone for one of them.
items.answer: Any three of FL, IN, KY, MI, TN, KS, NE, ND, SD, TX, ID, OR. E.g. Kentucky: Louisville (ET), Owensboro (CT).

items.question: A driver says his logbook shows 3 PM, but the local receiver clock says 4 PM. What is the likely explanation?
items.answer: The log uses the driver’s home-terminal time standard (e.g. Central) while the receiver is in Eastern Time.

items.question: Which is often the better choice out of Chicago, a slightly better-paying load to Miami or a load to Atlanta, and what question decides it?
items.answer: Often Atlanta, because it is a major hub with many reloads, while Miami can mean empty miles or a cheap load out. The question: “Where will the truck be after this load, and what can it do from there?” (Rates are compared properly in Module 7.)

items.question: State the 11-hour, 14-hour, 30-minute and 60/70-hour rules in your own words.
items.answer: 11 h driving after 10 h off; no driving after the 14th hour on duty; 30-min break after 8 cumulative hours of driving; no driving after 60 h / 7 days or 70 h / 8 days on duty.

items.question: Does the 14-hour window stop while the driver waits at a dock? Why does that matter?
items.answer: No. Waiting eats the window, so the driver loses driving hours and the next appointment may fail.

items.question: What counts as the 30-minute break?
items.answer: Any 30 consecutive minutes not driving: off duty, sleeper, on-duty-not-driving (e.g. loading), or a mix.

items.question: What resets the weekly cycle completely?
items.answer: A 34-hour (or longer) off-duty restart.

items.question: Describe the sleeper-berth split and one pairing that works.
items.answer: ≥ 7 h in the sleeper + ≥ 2 h off duty or sleeper, total ≥ 10 h (e.g. 7/3 or 8/2). Paired correctly, neither period counts against the 14-hour window.

items.question: What was wrong with “600 legal miles / 10 hr” in the old manual?
items.answer: The law limits hours, not miles, and 600 miles in 10 h requires a 60 mph average: unrealistic without speeding or violations.

items.question: Which planning speed does this module use, and roughly how many miles is a full solo driving day?
items.answer: 50 mph → about 500–550 miles on a full driving day.

items.question: Name four things an ELD records automatically or displays to the dispatcher.
items.answer: Any four: duty status, driving time, location, engine hours/miles, remaining drive/shift/break/cycle time.

items.question: What must a driver do if his ELD malfunctions?
items.answer: Note it, notify the carrier in writing within 24 h, reconstruct the current day + previous 7 days, keep paper logs until repaired.

items.question: Which time zone does a driver’s log use?
items.answer: The time standard of the driver’s home terminal.

items.question: What is coercion under 49 CFR 390.6, and who can be responsible?
items.answer: Forcing a driver to break safety rules (e.g. HOS). Motor carriers, shippers, receivers and transportation intermediaries (and their agents) can be responsible.

items.question: An ETA shows arrival 20 minutes before the appointment. What is your decision and what do you say?
items.answer: Only if. Ask the broker for a later window or FCFS; tell the carrier the risk. A 20-minute buffer is not enough.

items.question: What is the difference between a USDOT number, an MC number and authority status?
items.answer: USDOT = identity and safety record; MC = operating authority to haul for hire; status = whether that authority is active today.

items.question: Did Motus eliminate MC numbers? What did it change?
items.answer: No. Docket numbers are still issued and existing numbers don’t change. Motus added USDOT suffixes for new registrants, Login.gov identity checks, one docket per new authority, and pending-reason displays.

items.question: Which two FMCSA lookups do you use, and what does each show?
items.answer: SAFER: identity, size, inspections, crashes, rating, operating status. L&I: authority types and statuses, insurance filings, BOC-3.

items.question: What is the FMCSA minimum liability for a general-freight carrier, and what do brokers usually ask?
items.answer: $750,000 BIPD for general freight; brokers usually want $1,000,000 auto liability and often ≥ $100,000 cargo.

items.question: Why can a COI be current on paper but not valid?
items.answer: A COI is information only; the policy can be cancelled after printing, or the truck may not be on it. Verify with the agent.

items.question: What does “scheduled autos” mean for a dispatcher?
items.answer: Only the trucks listed on the policy are covered. The dispatched truck must be on the schedule.

items.question: What does an NOA tell a broker, and what happens if it is ignored?
items.answer: Pay the factoring company, not the carrier. If ignored, the broker may have to pay twice.

items.question: Name four things a dispatch agreement should cover.
items.answer: Any four: parties; services; authority to sign; compensation paid by the carrier only; carrier decides on loads; no brokering; payments go directly to carrier or factor; term; confidentiality.

items.question: Name five document red flags.
items.answer: Any five: names don’t match; expired COI; insured blank; truck not on policy; cargo exclusions; authority inactive; contact mismatch; surprise NOA; bank-change request by email.

items.question: Why must packets be sent only through verified channels?
items.answer: Packets hold tax IDs and bank details. Fraudsters use them to impersonate carriers and redirect payments.

items.question: Why is a load board posting not a booking?
items.answer: It is only an advertisement. Details and rates can change; the deal is made by phone, email or book-now, and is binding only with a signed rate confirmation.

items.question: What do DH-O and DH-D mean? What happens if you set DH-O too high?
items.answer: Deadhead to origin / from destination. Too high = more loads, but more unpaid miles and hours.

items.question: What does a blank destination mean? How would you search the whole Southeast in one go?
items.answer: Anywhere. Use zones: Z3 (and Z2).

items.question: What does the “Age” column tell you, and why do fresh loads matter?
items.answer: Time since posted or refreshed. Old loads are often covered; fresh loads get booked quickly.

items.question: What does DAT’s credit score measure? What is DTP?
items.answer: Creditworthiness from days-to-pay trends, collections, bankruptcies (via Equifax). DTP = average days to pay.

items.question: A load shows $1,800 for 700 loaded miles; the truck is 50 miles away. What is the rate per total mile?
items.answer: $1,800 ÷ 750 = $2.40 per total mile.

items.question: Why post a truck as well as searching?
items.answer: Brokers searching trucks (including for unposted freight) can find and call you.

items.question: What should you do with a truck posting when the truck gets booked?
items.answer: Remove or update it immediately.

items.question: List the five-filter scan.
items.answer: Can we haul it? Get there? Deliver it? Does it go somewhere good? Is it worth calling (rate, broker)?

items.question: Why search the next leg before booking the first load?
items.answer: A good outbound load into a dead market can lose money on the next leg. Knowing the reload options sets its real value.

items.question: Name three signals Truckstop shows about brokers or loads.
items.answer: Any three: bond backing, RMIS verification, factorable / new / private tags, rate insights, broker ratings.

items.question: A broker with no credit history posts a rate much higher than others. What do you think, and what do you do?
items.answer: Possible fraud or bait. Verify identity and authority carefully (Module 8), check with the factor, or skip it.

items.question: What is cost per mile? Why do we divide by total miles, not loaded miles?
items.answer: All costs ÷ all miles for a period. Empty miles cost fuel, pay and wear too, so leaving them out makes the truck look cheaper than it is.

items.question: Name three fixed costs and three variable costs.
items.answer: Fixed: truck payment, trailer payment, insurance, ELD/phone/board seat, permits. Variable: fuel, driver pay per mile, repairs, tyres, tolls.

items.question: Why does fixed cost per mile fall when the truck runs more miles?
items.answer: The weekly fixed amount is shared across more miles: $1,300 ÷ 2,000 = $0.65, ÷ 3,000 = $0.43.

items.question: Diesel rises from $5.00 to $6.38. How much does Truck 12’s fuel cost per mile change (6.5 mpg)?
Write the break-even formula. Why divide by (1 − fee %) instead of adding the fees?
items.answer: Break-even = cost per mile ÷ (1 − fee %). Fees are a percentage of the rate, and the rate is the unknown. Adding the fees to the cost undercounts them.

items.question: What are Truck 12’s operating cost, break-even and target minimum?
Calculate DAT’s fuel surcharge at $6.00 diesel and 6.0 mpg.
What is the difference between an all-in rate and linehaul + FSC?
items.answer: All-in = one total that already includes fuel. Linehaul + FSC = base pay plus a separate fuel amount; convert to all-in to compare.

items.question: What does a rate tool’s low–average–high range show? What minimum data does DAT RateView need to show a lane?
items.answer: The spread of recently reported paid rates (middle 50%) around the average. RateView needs at least 7 records from 3 different companies.

items.question: Define load-to-truck ratio. Why compare a market with its own history?
items.answer: Load posts ÷ truck posts for one market and equipment type. Levels differ by market and equipment (flatbed runs much higher than van), so “high” only means high compared with that market’s normal.

items.question: Give two reasons a load with a lower rate per mile can be the better choice.
items.answer: It leads to a strong reload or good end location; it uses fewer days (more per day); it fits the driver’s hours; it avoids a weak market.

items.question: What two deductions are on the Ship Express rate con, and how much money are they?
items.answer: $150 if tracking is refused or disabled; $150 if POD is not sent within 72 hours. $300 total.

items.question: What is double brokering, and why does the carrier often end up unpaid?
items.answer: Re-selling a load you took as a carrier, often via stolen identities. The real broker pays whoever it contracted with (the fraudster), who never pays your carrier.

items.question: Name four of the twelve red flags.
items.answer: Any four: rate far above market; brand-new authority; free or lookalike email; cell-only; pressure; hide your identity; new bank details; asks for logins; pickup changes; names don’t match; odd equipment; asks you to pay.

items.question: Which two FMCSA lookups confirm a broker’s authority and financial security? Which forms should you see?
items.answer: SAFER (entity type BROKER, broker authority active) and L&I (BMC-84 surety bond or BMC-85 trust fund, $75,000, no cancellation).

items.question: Under the rule in force since 16 January 2026, what happens when a broker’s security drops below $75,000?
items.answer: The provider notifies FMCSA; FMCSA notifies the broker, who has 7 business days to restore it or show an error; otherwise its authority is suspended.

items.question: Someone emails claiming to work for a broker you know. How do you verify them?
items.answer: Find the broker’s phone yourself (website, SAFER, board profile), call, and ask for the person by name. Compare the email domain with the website.

items.question: The BOL at pickup names a different carrier than yours. What do you tell the driver, and what do you do?
items.answer: “Don’t leave yet.” Call the broker on its official number (and the shipper if needed), tell Mike, and move only when it’s resolved in writing.

items.question: Name three places FMCSA says to report freight fraud.
items.answer: FMCSA NCCDB (nccdb.fmcsa.dot.gov), FMCSA Contact Center 1-800-832-5660, FTC, FBI IC3 or state attorney general, DOT OIG hotline.

items.question: Why can’t a dispatcher move a load from one of their carriers to another?
items.answer: It is brokering: arranging transport by another carrier for compensation requires broker registration and $75,000 security (49 U.S.C. 14916).

items.question: What is a walk-away number, and where does it come from?
items.answer: The lowest rate you’ll accept: usually break-even × total miles (Module 7), lower only when the carrier agrees for a strategic reason such as a strong reload.

items.question: What does “anchor with a reason” mean? Give an example sentence.
items.answer: Open with a number backed by facts. “For 727 miles with a same-day pickup I need $2,000. The lane has been around $2.60 a mile.”

items.question: Name three things you can negotiate besides the rate.
items.answer: Detention terms, lumper paid, quick pay, stop pay, pickup window, a backhaul.

items.question: What must you confirm before asking for the rate confirmation?
items.answer: All-in total, appointments, commodity and weight, accessorials, payment terms, carrier approval, setup.

items.question: Name the eight steps in a load’s life and the document each produces.
items.answer: (Combined answer 1–4) See page 4 (steps) · signed rate con = contract; only people the carrier authorizes sign · tracking deductions, POD deadlines, fines, liability, no TONU · driver info with time zones; rate at carrier’s choice.

items.question: Why must the rate con be signed before dispatch, and who may sign it?
items.answer: (Combined answer 1–4) See page 4 (steps) · signed rate con = contract; only people the carrier authorizes sign · tracking deductions, POD deadlines, fines, liability, no TONU · driver info with time zones; rate at carrier’s choice.

items.question: Name three rate con clauses that commonly cost carriers money.
items.answer: (Combined answer 1–4) See page 4 (steps) · signed rate con = contract; only people the carrier authorizes sign · tracking deductions, POD deadlines, fines, liability, no TONU · driver info with time zones; rate at carrier’s choice.

items.question: What belongs on a dispatch sheet? What might be left off, and who decides?
items.answer: (Combined answer 1–4) See page 4 (steps) · signed rate con = contract; only people the carrier authorizes sign · tracking deductions, POD deadlines, fines, liability, no TONU · driver info with time zones; rate at carrier’s choice.

items.question: What must a bill of lading show under 49 CFR 373.101?
items.answer: (Combined answer 5–8) Consignor/consignee, origin/destination, packages, description, weight/volume · shipper load and count when the driver couldn’t see or count · any change to the plan, delay, damage, refusal · counts match, nothing short/damaged, signed; for damage: photos, exact note, call broker.

items.question: What does SLC mean, and when should the driver write it?
items.answer: (Combined answer 5–8) Consignor/consignee, origin/destination, packages, description, weight/volume · shipper load and count when the driver couldn’t see or count · any change to the plan, delay, damage, refusal · counts match, nothing short/damaged, signed; for damage: photos, exact note, call broker.

items.question: When should you call the broker instead of sending a message?
items.answer: (Combined answer 5–8) Consignor/consignee, origin/destination, packages, description, weight/volume · shipper load and count when the driver couldn’t see or count · any change to the plan, delay, damage, refusal · counts match, nothing short/damaged, signed; for damage: photos, exact note, call broker.

items.question: What makes a POD “clean”? What do you do if freight is damaged?
items.answer: (Combined answer 5–8) Consignor/consignee, origin/destination, packages, description, weight/volume · shipper load and count when the driver couldn’t see or count · any change to the plan, delay, damage, refusal · counts match, nothing short/damaged, signed; for damage: photos, exact note, call broker.

items.question: Which documents go with an invoice?
items.answer: (Combined answer 9–12) Invoice, signed rate con, signed BOL/POD, receipts, detention proof · to the factor named in the NOA, so the broker pays the right party · 1 year · 10:00 PM PKT Thursday.

items.question: If the carrier factors, where does the invoice go, and why?
items.answer: (Combined answer 9–12) Invoice, signed rate con, signed BOL/POD, receipts, detention proof · to the factor named in the NOA, so the broker pays the right party · 1 year · 10:00 PM PKT Thursday.

items.question: How long must a carrier keep bills of lading under 49 CFR 379?
items.answer: (Combined answer 9–12) Invoice, signed rate con, signed BOL/POD, receipts, detention proof · to the factor named in the NOA, so the broker pays the right party · 1 year · 10:00 PM PKT Thursday.

items.question: Convert Thursday 1:00 PM Eastern (U.S. summer time) to Pakistan time.
items.answer: (Combined answer 9–12) Invoice, signed rate con, signed BOL/POD, receipts, detention proof · to the factor named in the NOA, so the broker pays the right party · 1 year · 10:00 PM PKT Thursday.

items.question: Define detention, layover, TONU and lumper.
items.answer: Detention: paid waiting after free time. Layover: held overnight or a day. TONU: truck ordered, not used (cancelled after dispatch). Lumper: paid unloading crew.

items.question: When does the detention clock usually start? Why doesn’t arriving early count?
items.answer: Usually at the appointment time (or arrival, if later). Arriving early is the carrier’s choice, not the facility’s delay.

items.question: Name three things you need to get detention paid.
items.answer: Terms on the rate con, times proven (tracking, BOL in/out), notice to the broker when required; then invoice with proof.

items.question: What does 49 U.S.C. 14103 say about loading and unloading help?
items.answer: A shipper or receiver that requires loading/unloading help must provide it or pay for it, and coercing a carrier to load or unload is unlawful.

items.question: What must happen before a driver pays a lumper?
items.answer: Driver calls you; you confirm with the broker who pays and how; payment method agreed; receipt obtained.

items.question: Give your first three actions when a truck is running late.
items.answer: Work out an honest ETA with hours, call the broker before the appointment, confirm in writing and ask for a new time.

items.question: After a breakdown, who decides what happens to the freight, and why can’t your carrier hand it to another truck on its own?
items.answer: The broker (with its customer). Handing the load to another carrier without the broker arranging it is brokering.

items.question: What evidence protects the carrier in a reefer temperature dispute?
items.answer: Setpoint on the BOL, unit download/temperature record, pulp temperatures, precool proof, times and messages.

items.question: What is an “accident” under 49 CFR 390.5, and what should you never say after one?
items.answer: A fatality, an injury treated away from the scene, or a vehicle towed for disabling damage. Never admit fault, promise payment or guess.

items.question: What is the difference between a POD notation and a claim?
items.answer: A notation records what was seen at delivery; a claim is a written demand identifying the shipment, asserting liability and stating an amount (49 CFR 370.3).

items.question: Under the Carmack Amendment, what are the minimum periods to file a claim and to sue?
items.answer: At least 9 months to file a claim; at least 2 years to sue after written denial (49 U.S.C. 14706).

items.question: Under 49 CFR 370, how quickly must a carrier acknowledge and decide a claim?
items.answer: Acknowledge within 30 days; pay, decline or offer within 120 days, with written status every 60 days if not resolved (49 CFR 370.5, 370.9).
